source_refs.note: Chapter 15 exercise (PDF 333-335), solved: 9 MCQs keyed from the chapter (no key printed), 13 short and 3 descriptive questions with model answers. MCQ V carries a Book correction ('mobile phones' for mobile phases).

blocks.text: Q.1 Four choices are given for each question. Select the correct choice.

blocks.prompt: I. After the crystals are formed, they are typically separated from the mother liquor by:
blocks.explanation: When crystallization is complete, the mixture of crystals and mother liquor is filtered (through a Gooch crucible with a vacuum pump) (15.4.1); the liquid can also be poured off (decanted).

blocks.prompt: II. The comparative rates at which the solutes move in paper chromatography depend on:
blocks.explanation: Each component has its own retardation factor, Rf = distance moved by the component ÷ distance moved by the solvent. A larger Rf means the solute moves faster (15.3.3).

blocks.prompt: III. The method that can be used to separate two solid compounds with different solubilities in a solvent is:
blocks.explanation: In crystallization the less soluble compound crystallizes out on cooling, while the more soluble one stays in the mother liquor (15.2).

blocks.prompt: IV. It is suspected that a hand-written legal document has been changed by over writing some crucial figures. Which technique you will use to check the inks used at suspected places?
blocks.explanation: Inks are mixtures of dyes; chromatography separates them and identifies them by comparing spots and Rf values (15.3.4: dyes). Different inks give different patterns.

blocks.prompt: V. In chromatography, the components of the mixture are separated based on:

options.text: The interaction of the components with stationary as well as mobile phones

blocks.explanation: Chromatography depends on the distribution of each component between the stationary phase and the mobile phase; components that interact differently move at different rates (15.3).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Option (b) is printed "stationary as well as mobile phones"; it means mobile phases.

blocks.prompt: VI. The porous material used to separate the solid from the liquid during filtration is called the:
blocks.explanation: Filtration is done with a filter medium such as filter paper or a filter crucible (15.1). The liquid that passes is the filtrate; the solid left behind is the residue.

blocks.prompt: VII. The key difference between simple distillation and fractional distillation is the presence of a:

options.text: Condenser with a larger surface area.

blocks.explanation: Fractional distillation uses a fractionating (distillation) column packed with glass beads between the flask and the condenser, giving a large surface for repeated condensation (15.2.1).

blocks.prompt: VIII. The essential requirement for separating two liquids by simple distillation is that their boiling points should differ by at least:
blocks.explanation: The chapter takes a boiling-point difference of about 25 °C as the dividing value (15.2.1): liquids that differ by at least about 25 °C can be separated by simple distillation; closer boiling points need a fractionating column.

blocks.prompt: IX. In chromatography, a locating agent is used to:

options.text: Carry the separated components along the stationary phase.
Make colorless separated components visible for identification.
Prevent the sample from interacting with the stationary phase.

blocks.explanation: A locating agent (e.g. ninhydrin) reacts with colourless substances such as amino acids to give coloured spots that can be seen (15.3.2).

blocks.text: Q.2 Attempt the following short-answer questions:

blocks.prompt: a. Why is there a need to crystallize a crude product?
blocks.explanation: A crude product contains impurities (e.g. unreacted starting material, coloured matter). Crystallization purifies it: the pure compound crystallizes out on cooling, while soluble impurities stay in the mother liquor and insoluble ones are filtered off. It also gives well-formed crystals whose purity can be checked by melting point.

blocks.prompt: b. What is the function of fluted filter paper?
blocks.explanation: A fluted filter paper is folded like a fan with alternate ridges and depressions. It gives a larger filtering surface and lets air pass, so filtration through a conical funnel is much faster (15.1).

blocks.prompt: c. What is the difference between a Gooch crucible and sintered glass crucible?
blocks.explanation: Both are used for quick filtration by suction; the sintered glass crucible needs no preparation.

rows: Made of porcelain
Made of glass
Perforated bottom covered with paper pulp, filter paper or asbestos mat
Porous glass disc sealed into the bottom
Needs preparation before use
Ready to use; no preparation needed
Used for precipitates to be ignited at high temperature; with asbestos, for liquids that attack paper (conc. HCl, KMnO₄)
Used for general suction filtration

blocks.prompt: d. What type of mixtures are filtered through a Gooch crucible?
blocks.explanation:
1. Precipitates that must be ignited (heated strongly) at high temperature after filtration.
2. With an asbestos mat over the perforations: solutions that react with paper, e.g. concentrated HCl and KMnO₄ solutions.
It is also used to filter crystals from the mother liquor by suction (15.1, 15.4.1).

blocks.prompt: e. What is function of fractionating column during fractional distillation?
blocks.explanation: The column, packed with glass beads, gives a large surface area on which the rising vapour condenses and re-vaporizes again and again. The more volatile liquid (lower boiling point) reaches the top and distils first, the less volatile one runs back, so two miscible liquids with close boiling points are separated (e.g. ethanol 78 °C and water 100 °C; petroleum fractions).

blocks.prompt: f. What is the stationary phase in the paper chromatography?
blocks.explanation: The stationary phase is the water trapped (held) in the cellulose fibres of the chromatography paper. The paper itself is only the support; the mobile phase is usually an organic solvent immiscible with this water (15.3.1).

blocks.prompt: g. What will happen during paper chromatography if the components of the mixture have a comparable attraction for the stationary phase?
blocks.explanation: They will be distributed in the same way between the two phases, move at almost the same rate and have nearly the same Rf values. Their spots will overlap, so the components will not separate; a different solvent must be tried.

blocks.prompt: h. What is the meant by the term “developing the chromatogram” in paper chromatography?
blocks.explanation: Developing is the process of letting the solvent (mobile phase) rise through the paper so that the components separate into spots; the dried pattern is the chromatogram. If the spots are colourless, the chromatogram is then developed by making them visible, under a UV lamp or by spraying a locating agent such as ninhydrin (15.3.2).

blocks.prompt: i. What is the basic principle of paper chromatography?
blocks.explanation: Paper chromatography is partition chromatography: each component of the mixture is distributed (partitioned) between the stationary phase (water held in the paper) and the mobile phase (organic solvent). Components that are more soluble in the mobile phase move faster; those held more by the stationary phase move slower, so they separate with different Rf values.

blocks.prompt: j. Why water is not generally used as a solvent in paper chromatography?
blocks.explanation: The stationary phase is itself water held in the paper's cellulose fibres. The mobile phase must be immiscible with it so that the solutes can partition between two different phases. Water would mix with the stationary water, so there would be no partition and little separation.

blocks.prompt: k. Differentiate between adsorption and partition chromatography.
blocks.explanation: The difference is the nature of the stationary phase: solid in adsorption, liquid in partition chromatography.

rows: Stationary phase is a solid
Stationary phase is a liquid (a film on an inert solid)
Substances leave the mobile phase and are adsorbed on the solid surface
Substances are distributed throughout both the stationary and mobile phases
Examples: thin layer chromatography (TLC), column chromatography
Examples: paper chromatography, gas liquid chromatography

blocks.prompt: l. How can you check the purity of a compound with the help of paper chromatography?
blocks.explanation: Spot the compound beside a pure sample of the same substance and run the chromatogram. A pure substance gives only one spot, with the same Rf value as the pure sample. An impure substance gives more than one spot (15.3.3).

blocks.prompt: m. You have prepared a solid sample of glucosazone in the laboratory. How will you proceed to check the purity of the sample?
blocks.explanation:
(Glucosazone itself is beyond the chapter; the chapter's methods for a solid apply.)
1. Melting point: dry the crystals and find the melting point. A pure sample melts sharply at the literature value; an impure one melts over a range.
2. Mixed melting point: mix with a pure glucosazone sample; a sharp, unchanged melting point means the sample is pure.
3. Paper chromatography: run it beside pure glucosazone; one spot with the same Rf value shows purity.
If impure, recrystallize and test again.

blocks.prompt: Q.3 Differentiate simple distillation and fractional distillation in construction and applications.
blocks.explanation:
Simple distillation separates a solvent from a solution (or liquids with widely different boiling points); fractional distillation adds a fractionating column to separate miscible liquids with close boiling points.
Simple distillation (construction): distillation flask with boiling chips, heated gently by a burner; thermometer; water condenser (cold water in at the lower end, out at the upper end); receiving flask. The vapour passes straight into the condenser; the distillate collects in the receiver and the residue stays in the flask.
Fractional distillation (construction): the same set-up, but a fractionating (distillation) column packed with glass beads is fixed between the flask and the condenser, with the thermometer at its top. Vapour condenses and re-vaporizes many times in the column. The receiver is changed when the temperature rises (e.g. ethanol collected at 78 °C, then water at 100 °C).

rows: No fractionating column; vapour goes straight to the condenser
Fractionating column packed with glass beads between flask and condenser
Single vaporization and condensation
Repeated condensation and vaporization in the column
Separates a solvent from dissolved solids, or liquids with boiling points far apart (about 25 °C or more)
Separates miscible liquids with close boiling points
Applications: pure water from sea water; removing a solvent
Applications: ethanol from water; petroleum into petrol, diesel, kerosene, furnace oil

blocks.prompt: Q.4 Describe the criterion to choose the suitable solvent in the process of crystallization?
blocks.explanation:
The principle of crystallization is that the solute dissolves in a suitable solvent at high temperature and the excess comes out as crystals on cooling. So an ideal solvent should:
1. Dissolve a large amount of the substance at its boiling point and only a small amount at room temperature.
2. Not react chemically with the solute.
3. Either not dissolve the impurities, or keep them dissolved so they do not crystallize with the solute.
4. Deposit well-formed crystals of the pure compound on cooling.
5. Be inexpensive, safe to use and easily removable from the crystals.
Common solvents: water, absolute ethanol, chloroform, carbon tetrachloride and acetic acid. If no single solvent is suitable, a mixture of two or more miscible solvents is used. An inflammable solvent is heated on a water bath, not over a flame.
The solvent is chosen by trial: small amounts of the substance are tested with different solvents, cold and hot (beyond the chapter).

blocks.prompt: Q.5 What is the basic principle of paper chromatography? Give its three practical life applications.
blocks.explanation:
Principle: paper chromatography is partition chromatography. The stationary phase is water trapped in the cellulose fibres of the paper and the mobile phase is an immiscible organic solvent that rises up the paper by capillary action (ascending method). Each component of the mixture is distributed (partitioned) between the two phases in its own ratio, so the components move at different rates and form separate spots. Each has a definite Rf value:
Rf = distance travelled by the component from the original spot ÷ distance travelled by the solvent from the original spot
The Rf value is constant for a substance with the same stationary and mobile phases.
Practical applications:
1. Checking purity: a pure substance gives one spot; an impure one gives more (e.g. aspirin run beside pure aspirin and salicylic acid).
2. Identifying complicated chemicals such as dyes, drugs and pesticides by comparing Rf values with known samples; e.g. checking the inks of a suspected forged document.
3. Separation, isolation and purification of products in organic synthesis, and qualitative and quantitative analysis (e.g. amino acids made visible with ninhydrin).
